title: SYSK Selects: Fractals - Whoa
summary: Rerun of the 2012 Stuff You Should Know episode on fractals, presented as a Selects episode. Hosts explain fractals as self-similar, recursive shapes produced by iteration of simple formulas, and distinguish them from Euclidean geometry. They cover the coastline paradox (Lewis Fry Richardson), the Koch snowflake, Cantor set, Sierpinski gasket, and Benoit Mandelbrot's work and the Mandelbrot set, plus Julia sets. Applications discussed include CGI landscapes (Star Trek II landscape by Loren Carpenter), Nathan Cohen's fractal antenna for cell phones, the Menger sponge, fractal analysis of rainforest carbon capture, blood vessel and tumor detection with ultrasound, heart rhythm analysis, and a theory on why larger animals use energy more efficiently. The episode also covers an man who acquired fractal synesthesia after being hit on the head and draws fractals by hand. The episode closes with a listener mail about peanut allergies and flying.

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Selects episode from June 2012 on fractals. Josh and Chuck joke about the Mandelbrot set image, admit they are not mathematicians, and debate calculators in math class.

segments.title: Definition of fractals and self-similarity
segments.summary: The hosts define a fractal as a self-similar geometric shape that is recursive through iteration. They contrast fractal geometry with Euclidean geometry, using a mountain as an example, and note fractal dimension describes complexity. Ferns are cited as natural examples of self-similarity.

segments.title: Sierpinski gasket and Mandelbrot's explanation
segments.summary: Using Benoit Mandelbrot's explanation, the hosts describe the Sierpinski gasket as an example of how an initiator is replaced by a generator to build a fractal. They explain the iterative formula concept and the feedback loop.

segments.title: Coastline paradox and Lewis Fry Richardson
segments.summary: Lewis Fry Richardson found that measured coastline length depends on the ruler length and grows toward infinity while enclosing finite area. The hosts describe this as a paradox that inspired fractal thinking. They note earlier artists such as Hokusai depicted fractal patterns.

segments.title: Mandelbrot set and how it is colored
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Mandelbrot formula, z goes to z squared plus c, and how numbers either diverge to infinity or go to zero. Points are colored by how quickly they diverge, with black for those that stay bounded, and zooming reveals more detail.

segments.title: History of fractal mathematics and early CGI
segments.summary: Koch snowflake, Cantor set, and Julia sets are introduced as earlier theoretical work by mathematicians in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Computers in the late 1970s made the sets visible, and Loren Carpenter's fractal landscape work for the Star Trek II CGI shot is described.

segments.title: Fractal applications: antennas, Menger sponge, forests, medicine
segments.summary: Nathan Cohen's bent fractal antenna improved reception, leading to cell phone designs based on the Menger sponge. Fractal analysis is used to estimate rainforest carbon capture from a single tree, and ultrasound analysis of blood vessel patterns may help detect tumors. Fractal analysis of heartbeats is used to study arrhythmia.

segments.title: Animal energy use and fractal synesthesia
segments.summary: The hosts describe research suggesting larger animals use energy more efficiently through a recursive genetic pattern. They then describe a man who acquired fractal synesthesia after being hit on the head and now draws mathematically accurate fractals by hand. Chuck says he doodles fractals.

segments.title: Listener mail on peanut allergies and flying
segments.summary: Listener Ian Hammer writes about severe peanut allergy and flying after the Air Traffic Control episode, explaining that airborne peanut molecules can cause reactions and that hospital care may be hard to reach mid-flight.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts suggest listeners search for fractals on HowStuffWorks, invite feedback by Twitter, Facebook, and email, and sign off.
